Aramaic is an ancient Semitic language closely related to Hebrew. By the first millennium before the common era, it had become the lingua franca of the Near East. Though Hebrew remained the sacred language of Jewish scripture and law, Aramaic became increasingly important after the Babylonian exile in 586 BCE, when it was the administrative and commercial language of the Persian Empire. Portions of the Hebrew Bible, specifically sections of the books of Daniel and Ezra, are actually written in Aramaic, reflecting this postexilic context. The Kaddish, one of the most important prayers in Jewish liturgy, is predominantly composed in Aramaic rather than Hebrew, showing how deeply the language embedded itself in Jewish practice. Jesus and his disciples spoke Aramaic as their primary language; several Aramaic phrases are preserved in the New Testament, like "Abba," meaning father, and "Talitha koum," meaning rise up. After the Babylonian captivity, Aramaic persisted while Hebrew fell into disuse as a spoken language, becoming the vernacular of Jewish communities in the diaspora while Hebrew remained reserved for prayer and study.
